object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer account; everything hangs off it. Identified by a unique, sequential, never-reused six-digit account number.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.
Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: Six digit sequential identifier for an Account, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a given amount on a given cycle for a given product; identified by a subscription ID.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: Unique generated identifier for a Subscription, prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product offered by the company, identified by a product code. Currently three: CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: ProductCode
object_types.definition: Code identifying a Product.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact that says what the customer pays and how often; generates the invoice line. Identified by a plan code. Entitles exactly one feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.
And I mean the billing artefact. The thing that generates the invoice line.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: Code identifying a Price Plan, e.g. CORE-MO-49.

source_references.excerpt: CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: The feature bundle a customer gets -- how many seats, API access, SSO; the thing on the pricing page. Identified by name (Starter, Professional, Enterprise).

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO.
Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me. ... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: FeatureBundleName
object_types.definition: Unique name of a Feature Bundle (Starter, Professional, Enterprise).

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: Mandatory start date of a subscription.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: Optional end date of a subscription; present for fixed-term deals or set on cancellation.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. ... A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front, that's usually an enterprise deal.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The billing cycle of a subscription: monthly or annual.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: Status of a subscription: trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

object_types.name: PausedFlag
object_types.definition: A separate boolean indicating a subscription is paused; overlaps confusingly with status.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... It's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

object_types.name: MRR
object_types.definition: Monthly recurring revenue; derived from the price plan price normalised to a month and the billing period, not stored.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR. Monthly recurring revenue.
It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month. An annual plan at 490 is an MRR of 40.83.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, with its own identity, effective date, and requester. Belongs to exactly one subscription.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date... It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: Identifier for a Plan Change.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a plan change takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person who requested a plan change.

ambiguities.description: Three different concepts are all called 'plan' by different stakeholders: the billing artefact (PricePlan), the feature bundle (FeatureBundle), and a third informal 'plan' sales negotiates that often matches neither. The sales-negotiated 'deal' is not modeled at all -- is it a real business concept requiring its own object type, or purely informal?

source_references.excerpt: So we've got two things both called plan. ... We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.

ambiguities.description: When an account closes and the same company returns, they get a new account number and are treated as a new customer for reporting purposes, losing history. Is 'Account' truly the right entity for 'Customer' as a business concept, or should there be a separate 'Company'/'Customer' entity above Account to preserve continuity? This is flagged as a modeling tension between finance and product perspectives.

source_references.excerpt: If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting. ... Which drives me mad, incidentally, because from a product perspective it's the same company and we lose the history.

ambiguities.description: The frequency constraint 'one active subscription per account per product' depends on subscription status (active), but status is a separate attribute of Subscription rather than part of the ternary fact type used for the uniqueness constraint. The exact scope of 'active' (does it include trialing or past due?) is not fully clarified -- does the block apply only to status='active', or also trialing/past due subscriptions?

source_references.excerpt: So it's one active subscription per account per product. ... No. The system blocks it.

ambiguities.description: PausedFlag is described as a boolean separate from SubscriptionStatus, but it 'overlaps confusingly' with active status -- querying active subscriptions returns paused ones too. It's unclear whether Paused is mutually exclusive with any status, or can co-occur with all four statuses, and whether this needs a formal constraint (e.g., paused only valid when status=active).

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: The commercial/business rule for mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions (run to term vs prorated refund vs credit) is explicitly undecided and parked by the facilitator. The model captures only the current system behaviour (end date set to paid-through date, no refund mechanism), not the disputed business policy exemplified by four manual credits issued outside the subscription system.

source_references.excerpt: By finance and legal, not by us, and not today. ... Then I'm parking it explicitly. What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided.

ambiguities.description: A fourth product is 'in discovery' and not yet defined -- is ProductCode's value constraint (CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT) meant to be extensible, or is it truly fixed? Similarly the enumerated statuses/billing periods are stated as fixed today but might not remain so.

source_references.excerpt: Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: The relationship between Subscription and its 'current' PricePlan is maintained via a denormalised field populated by the PlanChange process, and Priya states 'if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug' -- this implies a derivation/consistency rule (current plan should equal the price plan from the most recent effective PlanChange) that is not formally modeled as a subset/equality constraint due to lack of clarity on how 'most recent effective' is computed for future-dated changes.

source_references.excerpt: So the subscription does carry a current price plan, and the change records are the history behind it. ... Correct. And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: PlanChange has both a 'made on' date (when someone made the change) and an 'effective date' (when it takes effect), but only effective date was captured as an explicit attribute; the 'made on'/creation date is mentioned but not clearly named as a distinct stored field -- should a separate CreatedDate/RequestedDate value type be modeled?

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.
